statement: In children and youth in the general population (special populations, such as children in care, left out of the estimates), fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD), the umbrella term for the effects of alcohol before birth, which includes fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), partial FAS and alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder, was estimated in one systematic review with meta-analysis and modelling (Lange et al., 2017; 24 studies, 1,416 children and youth with FASD aged 0 to 16, from 8 countries; no funding statement; no conflicts declared) at 7.7 per 1,000 worldwide (95% CI 4.9 to 11.7), about 8 in 1,000, and FAS alone, in a companion review by the same team (Popova et al., 2017; 62 studies from 19 countries; funded by the authors' institute; no competing interests declared), at 14.6 per 10,000 people (9.4 to 23.3), about 1.5 in 1,000 (editors' conversion). By WHO region, FASD per 1,000 and FAS per 10,000 were 7.8 and 14.8 in the African region, 8.8 and 16.6 in the Americas, 0.1 and 0.2 in the Eastern Mediterranean, 19.8 and 37.4 in the European region, 1.4 and 2.7 in South-East Asia, and 6.7 and 12.7 in the Western Pacific. These world and regional figures are mostly calculated, not counted: FASD was pooled from studies for 6 countries and FAS for 7, and for every other country (181 and 180 of 187) the reviews divided the estimated share of women who drank during pregnancy, itself mostly predicted (see the answer on drinking in pregnancy), by a fixed ratio from a few countries, 13 women who drank per child with FASD and 67 per child with FAS, so the world figures are close to the world drinking figure of 9.8% divided by 13 and by 67 (editors' arithmetic). These ratios are averages across countries, not the chance for any one pregnancy, and neither review could examine the amount, pattern or timing of drinking. In the 24 FASD studies, figures ranged from 0.1 per 1,000 in a national Australian study and 0.4 to 5.6 per 1,000 in three French clinic studies of newborns to 63.9 to 207.5 per 1,000 in six studies of school-age children in South Africa's Northern and Western Cape in which researchers sought out and examined children; pooled national estimates were 53.3 per 1,000 for Croatia, 45.0 for Italy and 111.1 for South Africa. In eight select studies of special populations (adopted children or children in care, a correctional population, Indigenous populations, a low-income rural population, people in psychiatric care), FASD figures ran from 40.0 to 521.1 per 1,000. The authors say the diagnostic systems used differ and lack reliability, that studies were often done where many cases were expected, and that self-reported drinking may be undercounted. The two reviews' ratios imply about 5 children with FASD for each child with FAS (67 / 13, editors' arithmetic), while the FAS review cites a ratio of about 9 or 10. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: FASD is the name for the range of effects of alcohol on a child before birth; FAS is one of the diagnoses within it. Two reviews by one team estimated that about 8 in 1,000 children and youth worldwide have FASD, and about 1.5 in 1,000 people have FAS; for FASD, from about 0.1 in 1,000 in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean region to about 20 in 1,000 in the European region. But FASD had been counted in only 8 countries. For most of the world, the team took the estimated share of women who drank in pregnancy and divided it by one fixed number from a few countries; that number is an average, not the chance for any one pregnancy. Where researchers did count, figures ranged from under 1 to about 208 in 1,000 children, depending on the place and the method, and the ways of diagnosing FASD differ.
population: Children and youth (aged 0 to 16.4 years) in the general population: for FASD, 24 studies from 8 countries (Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, Norway, South Africa, USA) published November 1973 to June 2015, using active case ascertainment or clinic-based methods with a stated diagnostic guideline or case definition; for FAS, 62 general-population studies from 19 countries, the primary analysis using active case ascertainment or clinic-based studies with a stated guideline or case definition; estimates for 187 WHO member states, most of them predicted; select studies of special populations reported separately (FASD)
exposure: Not studied directly; for predictions, each country's prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy (self-reported, mostly itself predicted; Popova et al., 2017)
comparator: None (a prevalence); special populations set against the global FASD estimate as multiples
outcome: Prevalence of FASD per 1,000 children and youth and of FAS per 10,000 people in the general population, by country, WHO region and worldwide, weighted by live births and labelled 2012
magnitude: Lange et al. 2017 (FASD per 1,000 children and youth, Table 2; 95% CI by Monte Carlo simulation): worldwide 7.7 (4.9–11.7); WHO African region 7.8 (5.4–10.7); Americas 8.8 (6.4–13.2); Eastern Mediterranean 0.1 (0.1–0.5); European 19.8 (14.1–28.0); South-East Asia 1.4 (0.6–5.3); Western Pacific 6.7 (4.5–11.7). Five highest countries, in alphabetical order: Belarus 36.6 (23.7–53.2; predicted), Croatia 53.3 (30.9–81.2; meta-analysis), Ireland 47.5 (28.0–73.6; predicted), Italy 45.0 (35.1–56.1; meta-analysis), South Africa 111.1 (71.1–158.4; meta-analysis); 76 of 187 countries above 10 per 1,000 (1%), almost all by prediction. Study level (Table 1, per 1,000): Australia 0.1 (national; 92 cases in 1,533,333) and 1.7; Canada 5.3; Croatia 40.8 and 66.8; France 0.4, 5.4 and 5.6 in newborns and 66.0 on Réunion Island (75 cases in 1,320, which is 56.8, editors' arithmetic); Italy 40.5 and 47.1; Norway 1.1; South Africa 63.9 to 207.5; USA 5.1 to 33.5. Ratio: 1 FASD case per 13 women who drank in pregnancy, which the authors turn into about 630,000 children born with FASD each year. Special populations (Figure 2 legend, per 1,000): 40.0 to 521.1 in eight select studies, 5.2 to 67.7 times the global estimate. Popova et al. 2017 (FAS per 10,000 people, Table): worldwide 14.6 (9.4–23.3); African 14.8 (8.9–21.5); Americas 16.6 (11.0–24.0); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2 (0.2–0.9); European 37.4 (24.7–54.2); South-East Asia 2.7 (1.3–8.1); Western Pacific 12.7 (7.7–19.4). Five highest countries, in alphabetical order: Belarus 69.1 (42.1–103.5; predicted), Croatia 115.2 (34.8–236.0), Ireland 89.7 (50.4–142.8; predicted), Italy 82.1 (42.1–134.6), South Africa 585.3 (430.7–761.7). Ratio: 1 FAS case per 67 women who drank in pregnancy (from Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea and the USA), which the authors turn into about 119,000 children born with FAS each year by applying the prevalence per 10,000 people to 81,536,534 live births. The FAS review cites an earlier estimate (Abel, 1995; not read) of 4.3% FAS among children born to women who drank heavily in pregnancy (on average two or more drinks a day, or five to six at a time; no drink size in grams). Editors' arithmetic: 14.6 per 10,000 is 1.5 per 1,000; 9.8% / 13 = 7.5 per 1,000 and 9.8% / 67 = 14.6 per 10,000; 67 / 13 = 5.2 FASD cases per FAS case.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Limitations stated by the authors: predictions rest on self-reported drinking in pregnancy, which may be underestimated; the studies used different diagnostic guidelines and case definitions, whose effect on the pooled prevalence depends on their sensitivity and specificity; not all studies were nationally representative, and some regionally confined studies may have been done where FASD was more prevalent; predicted values carry measurement error; timing, dose and frequency of exposure could not be examined; two newer South African studies (170 to 259 per 1,000) fell outside the search window. The authors also state that current diagnostic guidelines overlap but lack diagnostic reliability, and that their sensitivity and specificity are unknown for lack of an external standard.

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Methods › Meta-analyses, 5th and 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Of 11,110 records, 62 FAS studies were retained, with data from 19 countries in four WHO regions (African, Americas, European, Western Pacific): 22 used active case ascertainment, 20 passive surveillance, 14 were clinic-based and 6 used mixed methods, and 40 used an established diagnostic guideline or stated their case definition. FAS was pooled by meta-analysis for 7 countries (primary analysis: active case ascertainment or clinic-based studies with a stated guideline or case definition) and, for 180 countries, computed by applying a quotient of women who drank in pregnancy per FAS case to the country's drinking prevalence. The five highest country estimates per 10,000: Belarus 69.1 (42.1–103.5; predicted), Italy 82.1 (42.1–134.6), Ireland 89.7 (50.4–142.8; predicted), Croatia 115.2 (34.8–236.0) and South Africa 585.3 (430.7–761.7).

risk_of_bias.note: Both reviews are AMSTAR 2 critically low on their cards (sc_lange_2017, sc_popova_2017): protocols registered after the searches, no lists of excluded studies, heterogeneity reported only in the supplements, publication bias tested but not discussed (FAS) or dismissed in advance (FASD). In the primary studies, diagnostic systems differ and, the authors say, lack reliability; studies were often done where high prevalence was expected; an inclusion rule was not applied strictly (an Australian study partly based on passive surveillance), and one row of the FASD table is misprinted (Réunion Island). Counted once.

inconsistency.note: Counted FASD runs from 0.1 to 207.5 per 1,000 across studies and from 0.4 to 66.0 within France; age, setting and method explain the spread only in part, and neither article reports heterogeneity statistics. The two reviews' ratios imply about 5 FASD cases per FAS case, against the 9 or 10 the FAS review cites.

indirectness.note: The world and regional figures are not measurements but drinking-in-pregnancy prevalences (self-reported and mostly predicted) divided by one ratio from a few countries and applied to all others (181 and 180 of 187 countries); FAS is counted per 10,000 people in samples of children of various ages, and the yearly birth figures apply it to live births; one set of figures labelled 2012 pools studies from 1974 to 2013.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded separately: the intervals are wide (FASD 4.9 to 11.7 per 1,000; FAS 9.4 to 23.3 per 10,000) and are reported; they come from Monte Carlo simulation and leave out the error in the ratios themselves, which is counted under indirectness.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: test results are only in the supplements (not read).

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (a prevalence): it starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3). Rated down once each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness, which is below the floor, so very low. Status single study: each figure rests on one review (FASD on Lange et al., FAS on Popova et al.); the two share their team and their FAS search, and the FASD predictions are built on the FAS review's drinking estimates, so they are not independent, and they estimate different things, so they neither replicate nor contradict each other. FASD and FAS are kept in one claim because a person asks one question, FAS is part of FASD, and only together do the figures show that both world estimates are the same drinking figure divided by two different ratios. The most solid numbers are the pooled national estimates from active case-finding studies (Croatia, Italy, South Africa), which describe those countries' study areas, not the world. The Brazilian orphanage figure is left out: the FAS review gives FAS there as 3191 per 10,000 and the FASD review gives FASD in the same orphanage as 170.2 per 1,000, which cannot both be right.
